title: Here Comes the AI Worm: Preventing the Propagation of Adversarial Self-Replicating Prompts Within GenAI Ecosystems
pdf_path: papers/Here Comes the AI Worm_Preventing the Propagation of Adversarial Self-Replicating Prompts Within GenAI Ecosystems.pdf
threat_model_summary: An adversarial self-replicating prompt spreads through a GenAI ecosystem: an infected assistant retrieves or receives the worm, incorporates it into its output, and sends it to new recipients, who repeat the cycle. The attacker controls the initial payload and some content, not the model or mail infrastructure.
core_contributions: RAGworm: a self-replicating prompt attack against retrieval-augmented and email assistants
Evaluation across 15 models and applications, with 13 fully susceptible
A propagation estimate of about 20 new clients per infected client under stated assumptions
DonkeyRail: a content-similarity guardrail using BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE-L
TPR 1.0 at FPR 0.017 (BLEU) or 0.005 (combined metrics), with millisecond latency
limitations: The 20-new-client estimate is a simulation, not end-to-end multi-user observation
Super-linear spread is not directly measured; Figure 7 plots cumulative mail volume, not infected users
No adaptive attacks; prompt and payload are visible
Only Enron and Hillary datasets
No external guardrail baseline
Threshold tuned to TPR 1.0 on the test split, so FPR may be optimistic
Only the draft-generation channel is covered
The abstract says 1-3 days, while Figure 7 implies about a week to 20 days at realistic send rates
Model Independence is contradicted by Claude 0/5, o3-mini 2/5, and Gemini 1.5 Pro degradation
The title says preventing, while Section 6 calls DonkeyRail a mitigation, not prevention
theoretical_crypto_links: None; the three properties are natural-language definitions, not a security game, theorem, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: None; DonkeyRail is a BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE-L content-similarity classifier
DKIM/S-MIME or signatures would authenticate the sender domain and message integrity, not establish that the content is not an instruction
A compromised legitimate account can still send the worm, and a victim assistant's outbound signed message remains valid
evidence_refs: pp.1-14 attack, propagation model, guardrail, and limitations
p.15 references browsed only; no appendix

title: SecAlign: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Preference Optimization
pdf_path: papers/SecAlign_Defending Against Prompt Injection with Preference Optimization.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker injects instructions through the data channel of an LLM application. SecAlign fine-tunes the model with preference optimization so that it follows the legitimate instruction and ignores injected data instructions. The defense is empirical and assumes instruction and data are explicitly separated.
core_contributions: SecAlign: a preference-optimization defense against prompt injection
DPO-style training on secure/insecure response pairs
Evaluation on five open models with optimization-free ASR near zero and optimization-based ASR of 1-14%
Utility comparisons on instruction-following, BIPIA, SEP, and InjecAgent
Ablations of DPO, ORPO, and KTO with training-cost comparisons
limitations: Requires explicit instruction/data separation
Does not claim 100% security
Multi-turn settings, further fine-tuning, and multiple benign instructions are untested
Does not defend jailbreaks or data extraction
Preference data is static and does not cover richer RAG or agent templates
Multimodal inputs are not covered
The abstract says ASR below 10%, but Llama-7B reaches 14%
Limitations say defense is most effective at the end, while Table 3 shows middle ASR below end ASR
The appendix says zero ASR at all times, while Table 8 has 0.5/1 under the in-response criterion
The text says three fine-tuning baselines but lists five
The text says two Instruct models exceed 70% WinRate, but Mistral-7B-Instruct is 67.01%
The introduction says optimization-based ASR is consistently over 40% for prompting baselines, which were not tested with optimization-based attacks
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
DPO, ORPO, and KTO are machine-learning objectives, not cryptographic preferences or proofs
applied_crypto_links: None; no OAuth, TLS, signatures, TEE, zk, or capability tokens are used
A signed instruction channel would authenticate origin, not make the model follow only the legitimate instruction
evidence_refs: pp.1-13 defense, experiments, ablations, and limitations
p.15 appendix tables 6-8; p.14 references browsed only

title: SkillScope: Toward Fine-Grained Least-Privilege Enforcement for Agent Skills
pdf_path: papers/SkillScope_Toward Fine-Grained Least-Privilege Enforcement for Agent Skills.pdf
threat_model_summary: Agent skills may request or perform actions beyond the user's task scope, whether maliciously or through ambiguity. SkillScope statically analyzes skill graphs, replays them in a sandbox, uses an LLM judge to estimate action authorization, and rewrites SKILL.md and scripts with semantic guards. It is an offline policy-checking and artifact-rewriting pipeline, not a runtime reference monitor with cryptographic capabilities.
core_contributions: SkillScope: fine-grained, action-level least-privilege analysis for agent skills
An ecosystem measurement of 68,312 skills, with 8,328 candidates and 6,590 confirmed over-privileged
Skill-level F1 94.53% and action-level F1 94.74%
Constraint rewriting that suppresses 88.56% of action-in-task violations (472 to 54)
Utility preservation of 94.78% output equality and 93.17% core-trace equality on 249 tasks
limitations: Capability is an everyday notion of packaged action range, not a formal unforgeable capability
Authorization is an LLM-estimated semantic predicate, not an executable check
No cryptographic capability token, signature, or attestation
Runtime guards are natural-language plus if/else code interpreted by the agent, without an independent reference monitor
No integrity binding of the rewritten bundle, so scanning then tampering or publishing a new version can bypass it
No adaptive attacker evaluation
Residual violations remain: 13/95 skills and 54/472 action-in-task
Single default GPT-5.1 judge; no inter-annotator agreement
Benchmark construction validity and 200-skill scale are limited
Real-agent utility is not reported
Table 2 reports GPT-5.1 F1 80.31%, while the counts give about 80.40%
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no security game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
Auth_p is a semantic authorization predicate estimated by an LLM, not a cryptographic relation
applied_crypto_links: None; sandbox and platform permissions are OS/application access control, not cryptographic capabilities
Signatures or attestation could bind the exact scanned bundle to a publisher and prevent post-scan tampering, but cannot decide whether an action is within task scope
Unforgeable capability tokens with delegation and attenuation are our inference, not implemented
evidence_refs: pp.1-14 method, ecosystem measurement, evaluation, and limitations
pp.16-21 appendices A-H; p.15 references browsed only

title: PriMobiBench: Characterizing Visual Privacy Leakage in VLM-Driven Mobile GUI Agents
pdf_path: papers/PriMobiBench_Characterizing Visual Privacy Leakage in VLM-Driven Mobile GUI Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A VLM-driven mobile GUI agent observes screens containing personal data and may recognize and aggregate privacy attributes across frames. The study measures recognition and profile construction in a synthetic benchmark; there is no adaptive attacker or network exfiltration measurement.
core_contributions: PriMobiBench: 320 samples and 2,960 privacy elements across 16 Android apps
Five privacy categories, 25 attributes, and 30 visual presentation forms
Recognition rates of 0.438-0.825 and profile construction of 0.401-0.712 across models
Mitigation study with segmentation and pixelation, reducing profile success by up to 57.9%
A 16-participant user study on perceived risk
limitations: Synthetic profiles and in-painted elements raise construct-validity concerns
No actual exfiltration or network measurement
No adaptive adversary
Privacy evaluation uses base VLMs while task evaluation uses agent frameworks
GPT-5-mini is both judge and evaluated model
Recognition numbers conflict across text, Figure 3, and Table 5
Gemma3-27B appears as 0.499, 0.550, and 0.652 in different places
The abstract combines 57.9% profile reduction (segmentation-only, 16.7-20.4% task loss) with about 8% utility loss (task-relevance filtering, up to 46.6% profile reduction)
Prompt explicitly forbids inference, yet inference-based recognition is reported
Profile prompts provide a closed attribute list, so this is attribute filling, not open-ended profiling
No confidence intervals or significance tests for main results
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, theorem, proof, or reduction
No differential privacy, k-anonymity, or cryptographic anonymity is defined or measured
applied_crypto_links: None; segmentation and mosaic blurring are pixel/semantic obfuscation, not provable anonymization
Differential privacy appears only as a one-line future-work suggestion
No encryption, TEE, or access control is evaluated
evidence_refs: pp.1-14 benchmark, recognition, profiling, mitigation, and limitations
pp.16-23 appendices A-F; p.15 references browsed only

title: Safeguarding LLM Agents against Long-Horizon Threats via Shadow Memory
pdf_path: papers/Safeguarding LLM Agents against Long-Horizon Threats via Shadow Memory.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker pursues a harmful goal across many turns, so no single action looks malicious. ShadowMem maintains a private semantic memory of the agent's trajectory and uses an RL-trained LLM monitor to detect long-horizon attacks before the harmful action. The defense is semantic and does not assume tamper-proof memory.
core_contributions: ShadowMem: a private shadow-memory and RL-trained monitor for long-horizon agent threats
SHADE-Arena ASR reduced from 100% to 8.3% with 94.4% benign utility
AgentDojo ASR of 0.7/0.4/0.0 across three backbones
Adaptive and white-box evaluations with ASR of 12.5-25% and 4.2%
About 6.13 s additional cost per task
limitations: Only STAC and PI2 attack families
At most 24 turns
Memory and judgment are not fully isolated and can be influenced by out-of-trajectory forged context
Fixed schema
Single agent
About 59 tasks in Evaluation I with no external baseline
Training and evaluation are same-source
LLM-as-judge labels are circular
Rejecting on a single false positive terminates the task
Local GPU cost is not included in the token cost
Isolation is described as partial rather than deterministic information-flow isolation
Lambda default 0.5 vs 1.0; token cost 3.6K vs 2.9K; default benign utility 56.8 vs 59.5
Memory update is called append-only in one example and overwrite in Eq. 2/D.1
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
Equations 1-3 are system equations and Equations 4-11 are RL objectives
applied_crypto_links: None; shadow memory has no hash chain, signature, or Merkle tree
Signature appears only as a metaphor for attack-pattern signatures
Spotlighting trusted instructions is a prompt-level distinction, not cryptographic authentication
evidence_refs: pp.1-14 threat model, method, evaluations, and limitations
pp.16-24 appendices A-F; p.15 references browsed only
